lessons.title: Maya, Aztec, Inca & Mound-Building Civilizations
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Maya, Aztec, Inca & Mississippian Civilizations
lessons.reading: Long before European arrival, the Maya built stone pyramids and calendars, the Aztecs built Tenochtitlan with floating chinampas, the Inca built Andes mountain terraces and roads, and Mississippian/Ohio mound builders constructed Cahokia and Serpent Mound.

principles.title: Early Civilizations of the Americas
principles.summary: Compare achievements of the Maya, Aztec, Inca, and Mississippian mound builders.

bank.prompt: Which civilization built stone pyramids and a 365-day calendar in Central America?
bank.explanation: The Maya civilization developed hieroglyphic writing, astronomy, and stone pyramids in Mesoamerica.

bank.prompt: What was the island capital city of the Aztec Empire in Mexico?
bank.explanation: The Aztecs built their grand capital, Tenochtitlan, on an island in Lake Texcoco.

bank.prompt: How did the Aztecs grow crops on shallow lake beds?
bank.explanation: Chinampas were fertile, man-made garden beds built in shallow lake water around Tenochtitlan.

bank.prompt: Where did the Inca Empire build its road network and terraced farms?
choices: The Andes Mountains of South America
The Great Plains of North America
bank.answer: The Andes Mountains of South America
bank.explanation: The Inca carved step-like terraces into steep Andes mountainsides and connected their empire with stone roads.

bank.prompt: What was the largest Mississippian mound-building city near the Mississippi River?
bank.explanation: Cahokia was a major Mississippian trade center famous for Monks Mound and earthen plazas.

bank.prompt: Why did the Inca cut flat steps (terraces) into steep mountain slopes?
choices: To create flat farmland and stop erosion
bank.answer: To create flat farmland and stop erosion
bank.explanation: Terrace farming kept soil and water in place so crops could grow on steep mountainsides.

bank.prompt: Which Ohio earthwork was built by ancient American Indian mound builders?
bank.explanation: Serpent Mound in southern Ohio is a famous effigy mound shaped like a giant curving snake.

bank.prompt: What knotted cords did the Inca use to record numbers and supplies?
bank.explanation: A quipu was a system of colored, knotted strings used by the Inca to keep numerical records.

lessons.title: American Indian Cultural Regions of North America
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Indigenous Cultural Regions of North America
lessons.reading: American Indian nations adapted to their environments: Eastern Woodlands peoples grew the Three Sisters (corn, beans, squash) and built longhouses; Plains nations used portable tipis; Southwest Pueblo peoples built adobe homes and irrigation canals.

principles.title: North American Cultural Regions and Adaptations
principles.summary: Explain how Indigenous groups adapted food and shelter to local environments.

bank.prompt: What were the "Three Sisters" crops grown by Eastern Woodland peoples?
bank.explanation: Corn, beans, and squash were planted together because corn stalks supported beans and squash shaded the soil.

bank.prompt: What type of multi-family bark homes did the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) build?
bank.explanation: Eastern Woodland Haudenosaunee families lived in long wooden frames covered with elm bark called longhouses.

bank.prompt: Why did Great Plains nations build portable tipis?
choices: Tipis were easy to move while following bison
Tipis were built from heavy stone blocks
bank.answer: Tipis were easy to move while following bison
bank.explanation: Plains nations used portable cone-shaped tipis made of poles and bison hides during seasonal hunts.

bank.prompt: How did Ancestral Pueblo peoples in the arid Southwest water their crops?
choices: Irrigation canals that directed scarce water
bank.answer: Irrigation canals that directed scarce water
bank.explanation: Southwest peoples adapted to dry desert climates by building irrigation ditches and adobe homes.

bank.prompt: What natural resource was most important to Pacific Northwest Coast cultures?
bank.explanation: Pacific Northwest nations used giant cedar trees for plank houses and canoes and fished for salmon.

bank.prompt: What was the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy?
choices: A peaceful alliance of American Indian nations
A gold mine in South America
bank.answer: A peaceful alliance of American Indian nations
bank.explanation: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy united nations under the Great Law of Peace to make shared decisions.

bank.prompt: What material did Southwest Pueblo builders use for cool, sturdy homes?
bank.explanation: Adobe bricks made from clay, sand, and straw kept Southwest homes cool in desert heat.

bank.prompt: Why did different American Indian cultural regions have different foods and homes?
choices: They adapted to local climate and natural resources
They all lived in identical climates
No plants grew in North America
bank.answer: They adapted to local climate and natural resources
bank.explanation: Indigenous peoples shaped their shelter, clothing, and food around the environment of their region.

units.title: Unit 2: Exploration, Thirteen Colonies, U.S. Founding & Geography

lessons.title: Exploration, Thirteen Colonies & the American Revolution
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Colonies, Revolution & the U.S. Constitution
lessons.reading: European exploration started the Columbian Exchange. English colonists founded Jamestown (1607) and Plymouth (1620). Later, colonists protested British taxes without representation, adopted the Declaration of Independence (1776), and created the U.S. Constitution with three branches of government.

principles.title: Exploration, Colonial America, and Constitutional Government
principles.summary: Trace the Columbian Exchange, Jamestown/Plymouth, the Revolution, and the three branches of government.

bank.prompt: What was the Columbian Exchange?
choices: Exchange of plants, animals, and goods across oceans
A treaty between Ohio and Canada
A gold coin used in Boston
bank.answer: Exchange of plants, animals, and goods across oceans
bank.explanation: The Columbian Exchange moved crops, livestock, people, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia.

bank.prompt: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America (1607)?
bank.explanation: English colonists founded Jamestown in Virginia in 1607 as their first permanent settlement.

bank.prompt: Why did the Pilgrims sign the Mayflower Compact in 1620?
choices: To agree on fair laws and self-government
To ban farming in New England
bank.answer: To agree on fair laws and self-government
bank.explanation: The Mayflower Compact was an early agreement establishing self-government in Plymouth Colony.

bank.prompt: Why did American colonists protest British taxes like the Stamp Act?
choices: They had no elected representatives in Parliament
They wanted higher taxes on tea
They wanted to return to England
bank.answer: They had no elected representatives in Parliament
bank.explanation: Colonists argued "no taxation without representation" because they had no voice in the British Parliament.

bank.prompt: Who was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence in 1776?
bank.explanation: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence explaining why the colonies broke away from Britain.

bank.prompt: According to the Declaration of Independence, what are people’s natural rights?
choices: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
bank.answer: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
bank.explanation: The Declaration states that all people have natural rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

bank.prompt: What are the three branches of the U.S. government under the Constitution?
bank.explanation: The Constitution divides power among the Legislative (Congress), Executive (President), and Judicial (Courts) branches.

bank.prompt: What do the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution protect?
choices: Individual freedoms in the Bill of Rights
bank.answer: Individual freedoms in the Bill of Rights
bank.explanation: The Bill of Rights guarantees freedoms such as speech, religion, press, and fair trials.

lessons.title: Western Hemisphere Geography, Trade & Opportunity Cost
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Latitude, Longitude, Trade & Opportunity Cost
lessons.reading: Latitude measures degrees north or south of the Equator (0°), and longitude measures degrees east or west of the Prime Meridian. Regions near the Equator are warmer. In economics, opportunity cost is the next best choice you give up when making a decision.

principles.title: Latitude, Longitude, Specialization, and Opportunity Cost
principles.summary: Use latitude/longitude and explain specialization, trade, and opportunity cost.

bank.prompt: What do lines of latitude measure on a globe or map?
choices: Distance north or south of the Equator
Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
bank.answer: Distance north or south of the Equator
bank.explanation: Parallels of latitude run east-west and measure degrees north or south of the Equator.

bank.prompt: What do lines of longitude measure on a globe or map?
choices: Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
Distance north or south of the Equator
bank.answer: Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
bank.explanation: Meridians of longitude run from pole to pole and measure degrees east or west of the Prime Meridian.

bank.prompt: How does climate generally change as you travel closer to the Equator?
bank.explanation: Low latitudes near the Equator receive direct sunlight all year, creating warm tropical climates.

bank.prompt: In economics, what is "opportunity cost"?
choices: The next best choice you give up when deciding
The price tag printed on a toy
Money saved in a piggy bank
A free gift from a friend
bank.answer: The next best choice you give up when deciding
bank.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the second-best option you give up when you make a choice.

bank.prompt: Why do countries in the Western Hemisphere specialize and trade?
choices: Different regions produce goods they make best
Trade reduces the variety of goods
No country grows its own food
bank.answer: Different regions produce goods they make best
bank.explanation: Specialization and trade let regions exchange products they make efficiently for goods they need.

bank.prompt: What happens to orange prices if a frost ruins the crop?
choices: Prices rise because supply is lower
bank.answer: Prices rise because supply is lower
bank.explanation: When supply drops and demand stays the same, scarcity causes the price of a good to increase.

bank.prompt: Which 0° latitude line divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
bank.explanation: The Equator sits at 0 degrees latitude halfway between the North and South Poles.

bank.prompt: Mia picks a book over a game. What is her opportunity cost?
bank.explanation: Because Mia chose the book, the board game she gave up is her opportunity cost.

bank.answer: Individual freedoms in the Bill of Rights
bank.explanation: The Bill of Rights guarantees freedoms such as speech, religion, press, and fair trials.

principles.title: Latitude, Longitude, Specialization, and Opportunity Cost
principles.summary: Apply map coordinates, climate patterns, supply/demand, and opportunity cost.

bank.prompt: What do lines of latitude measure on a globe or map?
choices: Distance north or south of the Equator
Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
bank.answer: Distance north or south of the Equator
bank.explanation: Parallels of latitude run east-west and measure degrees north or south of the Equator.

bank.prompt: What do lines of longitude measure on a globe or map?
choices: Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
Distance north or south of the Equator
bank.answer: Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
bank.explanation: Meridians of longitude run from pole to pole and measure degrees east or west of the Prime Meridian.

bank.prompt: How does climate generally change as you travel closer to the Equator?
bank.explanation: Low latitudes near the Equator receive direct sunlight all year, creating warm tropical climates.

bank.prompt: In economics, what is "opportunity cost"?
choices: The next best choice you give up when deciding
The price tag printed on a toy
Money saved in a piggy bank
A free gift from a friend
bank.answer: The next best choice you give up when deciding
bank.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the second-best option you give up when you make a choice.

bank.prompt: Why do countries in the Western Hemisphere specialize and trade?
choices: Different regions produce goods they make best
Trade reduces the variety of goods
No country grows its own food
bank.answer: Different regions produce goods they make best
bank.explanation: Specialization and trade let regions exchange products they make efficiently for goods they need.

bank.prompt: What happens to orange prices if a frost ruins the crop?
choices: Prices rise because supply is lower
bank.answer: Prices rise because supply is lower
bank.explanation: When supply drops and demand stays the same, scarcity causes the price of a good to increase.

bank.prompt: Which 0° latitude line divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
bank.explanation: The Equator sits at 0 degrees latitude halfway between the North and South Poles.

bank.prompt: Mia picks a book over a game. What is her opportunity cost?
bank.explanation: Because Mia chose the book, the board game she gave up is her opportunity cost.
